heroLead: Washam is a rail siding, not a town with a courthouse of its own - your mineral rights here run through Sweetwater County records in Green River, and the section lines still follow the old railroad pattern.
intro: Washam sits out in the open country of southern Sweetwater County, the kind of place that shows up on a plat map more than it does on a highway sign. There's no town government to speak of, but the ground underneath has been part of the Green River Basin's oil, gas, and trona story for close to a century.

This is core Union Pacific checkerboard territory. The original 1862 railroad grant handed the UP the odd-numbered sections in a strip across southern Wyoming, and the pattern is still stamped on every plat around Washam - private and federal sections alternating like a checkerboard, which is exactly what the old-timers call it. Whoever holds your mineral deed inherited that pattern whether they know it or not.

sections.heading: The Green River Basin Around Washam
paragraphs: Sweetwater County is Green River Basin bedrock - tight gas out of the Lance and Fort Union, deeper Frontier and Almond production, and a legacy of Wamsutter-area drilling that stretches back decades. Washam itself sits removed from the densest activity around Wamsutter and Table Rock, but it's inside the basin's broader productive fairway, and lease interest here tracks basin-wide gas prices more than any single well.

Add to that Sweetwater's trona beds - the county produces most of the nation's soda ash - and you've got a place where mineral ownership sometimes means more than oil and gas. If your deed language is broad ('all minerals'), it's worth checking whether it reaches the trona horizon too.

sections.heading: Checkerboard Ownership Means Title Work Isn't Optional
paragraphs: Because the UP grant alternated sections with the federal government, two neighboring quarter sections near Washam can have completely different ownership chains - one private mineral estate passed down through a family, the next controlled by the BLM. We run the deed history at the Sweetwater County Clerk's office in Green River before we quote anything, because the legal description on an old family mineral deed doesn't always match current section lines cleanly.

sections.heading: What a Sale Actually Looks Like
paragraphs: Most interests we see out of this part of the county are non-producing or lightly held - small fractional shares from a homestead-era mineral severance, sometimes split six or eight ways among heirs. We buy those outright, handle the closing paperwork, and record the assignment at the county clerk's office. If your interest has royalty history tied to it, we look at the decline curve on that production before we set a number, not a flat guess.

faqs.question: Is Washam an incorporated town with its own records?
faqs.answer: No. Washam is an unincorporated place in Sweetwater County. Deed and title records for property here are filed at the Sweetwater County Clerk's office in Green River.

faqs.question: Why does the checkerboard pattern matter for my mineral rights?
faqs.answer: It means ownership can change section to section. A tract next to yours might be federal minerals under BLM control while yours is privately held, so we verify your specific legal description rather than assuming based on the surrounding land.

faqs.question: Does my mineral deed cover trona along with oil and gas?
faqs.answer: It depends on how the deed is worded. Broad 'all minerals' language may reach the trona horizon; a deed that specifically says oil, gas, and hydrocarbons typically does not. We read the language before we make an offer.

faqs.question: What if my interest has never produced anything?
faqs.answer: We still buy non-producing interests. The offer reflects basin activity trends and your net mineral acreage rather than existing royalty income, since there isn't any to point to yet.
